Learning Objectives
Describe the etiology and pathoanatomy of isthmic spondylolisthesis.
Assess the natural history and symptomatology of isthmic spondylolisthesis.
Recognize the spinal and pelvic radiographic parameters of isthmic spondylolisthesis.
Describe classification systems for spondylolisthesis.
Review common treatment options for patients with isthmic spondylolisthesis.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Isthmic spondylolisthesis results from a defect in the pars interarticularis (spondylolysis).


Overview
Spondylolysis (Resource 1) is a defect in the pars articularis of a vertebra (Figure 1).
Spondylolysis can occur independently or in association with spondylolisthesis and often
occurs at the L5-S1 level. Spondylolisthesis is the forward displacement of one vertebra
with respect to the adjacent caudal vertebra. Spondyloptosis is defined as 100%
translation of one vertebra over the next caudal vertebra.1
Figure 1 Images of the spine of a 13-year-old girl who presented with back pain. A,
Sagittal CT scan shows a chronic-appearing L5 spondylolytic defect and increased
sclerosis about the L4 pars interarticularis. After a period of rest followed by extensive
core strengthening exercises, the patient successfully returned to all sports activity. B,
Lateral radiograph obtained via biplane x-ray imaging (EOS Imaging) at 2-year follow-up
demonstrates bilateral L5 pars defects and grade 1 spondylolisthesis; however, the
patient was asymptomatic. (Reproduced from Larson AE: Back pain, disk disease,
spondylolysis, and spondylolisthesis, in Martus JE, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update:
Pediatrics, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp
415-429.)
Epidemiology
Isthmic spondylolisthesis is the most common type of spondylolisthesis in children and young
adults.
It occurs in 5% of the population.

It is more common in Innuits and young males involved in repetitive hyperextension activities
(eg, gymnastics).

Epidemiology
Isthmic spondylolisthesis in children mainly occurs at L5-S1 (87%) but also has been
reported at L4-L5 (10%) and L3-L4 (3%).2 A defect in the pars interarticularis has never
been reported in a newborn. In a prospective study of 500 children, a prevalence of
spondylolysis of 4.4% by age 6 years, 5.2% by age 12 years, 5.6% by age 14 years, and 6%
in adulthood was reported.3 In the children with bilateral spondylolysis, 68% had
spondylolisthesis by age 6 years and 74% had the condition by age 18 years. A 45-year
follow-up study of 30 participants in whom spondylolysis had been diagnosed during
childhood showed that spondylolisthesis did not develop in eight of the participants with
unilateral defects, whereas 22 of the participants with bilateral spondylolysis had
spondylolisthesis.4 In these study participants, a slowing of slip progression occurred
with each decade until age 50 years.
Spondylolysis is highly prevalent in some Native American populations.5 An increased
prevalence of spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis also has been reported in athletes
who participate in certain sports, such as gymnastics;6 however, a more recent study did
not observe this association between increased occurrence and participation in
gymnastics (Video 1).

Classification and treatment of spinal deformity in the orthopaedic clinic. Presented at

March 12-16, 2019.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Associated conditions include spina bifida.
Isthmic spondylolisthesis most commonly occurs at L5-S1. L4-L5 isthmic slips are more
susceptible to progression because the iliolumbar ligament adds stability to the L5-S1
segment.
The alignment of the lumbar spine and, subsequently, the mechanical stresses at the
lumbosacral junction are altered by the morphology of the sacrum and pelvis. Other important
factors include the slip angle, sacral inclination, and the sacral slope.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Sagittal plane sacropelvic morphology and orientation are routinely measured using
pelvic incidence, sacral slope, and pelvic tilt (Figure 2).

Figure 2 Images show measurement of sagittal plane sacropelvic orientation and
morphology. A, Lateral view schematic drawing shows the lumbosacral junction with
standard parameters of pelvic morphology and spinopelvic balance in spondylolisthesis.
In low-grade spondylolisthesis, the subtype depends on whether the pelvic incidence (PI)
and the sacral slope (SS) are high or low. In high-grade spondylolisthesis, the subtype
depends on whether the pelvic tilt (PT) and SS are high or low. B through G, Lateral
radiographs demonstrate the six spinopelvic postures that have been described in
patients with spondylolisthesis. B, Low-grade spondylolisthesis with a low PI and a low
SS (nutcracker type). C, Low-grade spondylolisthesis with a normal PI and SS. D, Low-
grade spondylolisthesis with a high PI and a high SS (shear type). E, High-grade
spondylolisthesis with a balanced pelvis, a high SS, and a low PT. F, High-grade
spondylolisthesis with a retroverted pelvis, a low SS, a high PT, and a balanced spine. G,
High-grade spondylolisthesis with an unbalanced spine. (Panel A reproduced from
Larson AE: Back pain, disk disease, spondylolysis, and spondylolisthesis, in Martus JE, ed:

Pelvic incidence, a morphologic parameter, is specific to each individual and unaffected
by changes in body position. Pelvic incidence represents the arithmetic sum of the pelvic
tilt and sacral slope. Pelvic incidence is described as a line drawn from the center of the
femoral heads to the midpoint of the sacral end plate and a line perpendicular to the
center of the sacral end plate. Sacral slope is defined as the angle subtended by the
horizontal plane and the upper sacral end plate. Pelvic tilt is defined as the angle created
by a line from the midpoint of the sacral end plate to the center femoral heads and a
vertical plumb line (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Lateral radiographs of the spine of a patient with high-grade spondylolisthesis.
A, Radiograph demonstrates characteristic local deformity associated with high-grade
spondylolisthesis, including slippage, sacral doming, and lumbosacral kyphosis (LSK). B,
Increasing pelvic tilt and pelvic incidence (PI) occur as the patient attempts to
compensate by retroverting the pelvis. C, Full-length standing radiograph allows for
evaluation of global sagittal balance. Sagittal imbalance and hip flexion occur as the
patient attempts to compensate globally for the high degree of slip. (Reproduced from
Parent S, Labelle H, Thiong-Mac JM: Spondylolisthesis in children and young adults, in
Truumees E, Prather H, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 371-380.)

In children and adolescents without spondylolisthesis, sacropelvic morphology regulates
sacropelvic orientation, which greatly affects the shape and orientation of the spine,
especially lumbar lordosis.7,8 Sacropelvic morphology is different in healthy control
subjects than in patients with spondylolisthesis.9 Pelvic incidence also increases in direct
linear proportion to the severity of the spondylolisthesis.9 With the increasing severity of
the spondylolisthesis, the close relationship between sacropelvic and lumbar geometry
typical of normal healthy individuals is disturbed.7
In control subjects with abnormal sacropelvic morphology, a predisposition to altered
mechanical stresses in the lumbar spine and the lumbosacral junction appears to exist.
These individuals also seem to have a higher risk for spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis.
The shear stress on the L5-S1 disk tends to be increased by a high pelvic incidence
associated with a high sacral slope. This induces increased loading on the L5 pars
articularis.10 A low pelvic incidence may lead to repetitive impingement of the pars
interarticularis of L5 by the posterior facets of L4 and S1 during extension movements.10
Lumbosacral alignment and global sagittal alignment may be altered in the presence of
abnormal sacropelvic balance and progressive spondylolisthesis. In addition to the
translational slip of L5 on top of S1, an angular deformity appearing as lumbosacral
kyphosis can occur. Forward global spinal balance (as measured by a plumb line from C7
to the sacrum) and forward spinopelvic balance (as measured by a plumb line from C7 to
the hip axis) also may be observed, particularly in patients with high-grade
spondylolisthesis.7 In response to progressively abnormal sacropelvic, lumbosacral, and
global balance, the center of gravity of the torso tends to be displaced anteriorly. This
anterior displacement causes forward displacement of the anterior aspect of L5,
whereas the posterior aspect of L5 remains attached to the posterior soft tissues and
the L5-S1 facet (Video 2).

Video 2 Parent S: How spondylolisthesis can lead to a lifelong symptomatology, in
Choma TJ, mod: Applying deformity concepts to the degenerative spine practice.
Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
San Diego, CA, March 14-18, 2017.
Etiology
The exact etiology of spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis is unknown; however, it most likely is
multifactorial.
Various hereditary, traumatic, biomechanical, growth, and morphologic factors have been
proposed to play a role.

Etiology
Spondylolisthesis is believed to be related to an autosomal dominant genetic
predisposition with incomplete penetrance.11,12 An increased prevalence of
spondylolisthesis has been reported in members of the same family, ranging from 19%
to 69% in first-degree relatives. In addition, high-grade spondylolisthesis has been
reported in identical twins.13
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003014
8/28

Repetitive microtrauma has been suggested as a cause for spondylolisthesis via the
creation of a stress fracture of the pars interarticularis.14 The pars interarticularis (the
weakest region of the posterior neural arch) is subjected to high shear, compressive, and
tensile loads during flexion and extension movements.15 Athletes who participate in
sports that involve recurrent alternating flexion-extension spinal loading have a higher
risk for spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis. The prevalence of spondylolisthesis is
increased in this patient population.6
Under normal conditions, the facet joints at L5-S1 resist most of the shear force,
whereas most of the compression force passes through the disks. The facet joints are
not functional in patients with spondylolysis; therefore, most of the shear stresses at L5-
S1 are transferred to the disk, which predisposes patients to disk degeneration and
subsequent spondylolisthesis. In addition, forward displacement of the body of L5
distracts the pars defect because the posterior elements of L5 remain strongly attached
to the posterior ligaments and the erector spinae muscles. As spondylolisthesis
progresses, a further decrease in disk stiffness occurs, and stresses increase across the
lumbosacral junction.16 Varying degrees of facet, laminar, and end-plate dysplasia are
common in spondylolisthesis and disturb the normal posterior bony hook/catch at the
lumbosacral junction.3,17,18 In some patients with spondylolisthesis, the initially present
pars defect heals with elongation of the posterior elements.15
Natural History
Slip progression is most likely to occur in adolescents younger than 15 years, usually during
the adolescent growth spurt. With skeletal maturity, progression usually does not advance.
Slip progression occurs in approximately 20% of adults in their twenties. Slip progression is
related to progressive disk degeneration that renders the segment relatively unstable.
Classification
The Meyerding classification of isthmic spondylolisthesis is based on slip percentage.
The Wiltse classification divides spondylolisthesis into five major types (and several subtypes)
based on imaging study findings.

The Marchetti and Bartolozzi classification is an etiology-based prognosis system of
spondylolisthesis that divides types into two broad categories: developmental and acquired.

Classification
The Meyerding classification system is the simplest classification of spondylolisthesis19
(Figure 4). The classification system is based on the percentage of translation. Grade I
indicates a translation of the cranial vertebra of zero to 25%, grade II indicates a
translation of 26% to 50%, grade III indicates a translation of 51% to 75%, and grade IV
indicates a translation of 76% to 99%. Grade V was later added to describe ptosis of the
cranial vertebra.
Figure 4 Illustrations of the lumbar spine show the Meyerding classification system,
which provides a simple and common quantification of the slip of L5 and S1. A, Grade I
defines a slip from zero to 25%, grade II defines a slip from 26% to 50%, grade III defines
a slip from 51% to 75%, and grade IV defines a slip from 76% to 100%. B, To determine
the slip angle, a line is drawn parallel to the posterior aspect of the sacrum, with a
perpendicular line at the level of the cephalad border of the sacrum (because of
remodeling). Another line is drawn at the undersurface of the body of L5. This angle
represents the relationship of L5 to the sacrum. C, In higher grade slips, the sacrum
becomes more vertical and the kyphotic deformity increases, as measured by the sacral
inclination (unmarked line). D, Sacral slope is defined as the angle between the
horizontal reference line and the end-plate line of S1. (Reproduced from Ofiram E,
Garvey TA: Adult isthmic spondylolisthesis, in Spivak JM, Connolly PJ, eds: Orthopaedic
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:11 AM
AAOS | Adult Isthmic Spondylolisthesis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003014
10/28

Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2006, p 312.)
The Wiltse classification system divides spondylolisthesis into five major types (and
several subtypes) based on imaging study findings20 (Figure 5). The five types are as
follows: dysplastic, isthmic, degenerative, traumatic, and pathologic. In the dysplastic
type, a congenital defect of the lumbosacral facet joints is present, and the translation is
secondary to an abnormal neural arch. In the isthmic type, the lumbosacral facets are
normal, but the spondylolisthesis is caused by a defect in the pars interarticularis. The
isthmic type can be subdivided based on whether the pars fracture is lytic, elongated, or
acute. Degenerative spondylolisthesis results from chronic instability and intersegmental
degenerative changes. Traumatic spondylolisthesis results from an acute fracture of
posterior elements other than the pars interarticularis. The pathologic type is associated
with diffuse or local disease that compromises the usual structural integrity that
prevents slippage. Although this classification system is useful in classifying
spondylolisthesis by defect type, it is not helpful in treatment planning.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:11 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003014

Figure 5 Illustrations of the lumbar spine show the Wiltse classification of
spondylolisthesis. A, Normal. B, Type 1: dysplastic. C, Type IIA: break in the pars
interarticularis. D, Type IIB: elongated but intact pars interarticularis. E, Type IIC: acute
fracture. F, Type III: degenerative. G, Type IV: fracture other than the pars interarticularis.
H, Type V: pathologic. (Reproduced from Parent S, Labelle H, Thiong-Mac JM:
Spondylolisthesis in children and young adults, in Truumees E, Prather H, eds:
Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 371-380.)
The Marchetti and Bartolozzi classification system is an etiology-based prognosis system
of spondylolisthesis that divides types into two broad categories: developmental and
acquired.21 Based on the severity of bony dysplasia in the L5 and S1 vertebrae and the
risk of additional slippage, developmental spondylolisthesis is categorized into two major
types: high dysplastic and low dysplastic. Dysplastic characteristics commonly observed
in both variants include dysplastic facet joints; however, high dysplastic spondylolisthesis
also is associated with substantial lumbosacral kyphosis, trapezoidal L5 vertebra,
hypoplastic transverse processes, and sacral doming with verticalization of the sacrum.

9/3/26, 7:11 AM
AAOS | Adult Isthmic Spondylolisthesis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003014
12/28

Characteristics of low dysplastic spondylolisthesis include preservation of the shape of
the L5 vertebral body and sacral dome, a relatively normal lumbosacral profile, and
preservation of a flat sacroiliac upper end plate.
Acquired spondylolisthesis occurs secondary to trauma, surgery, a pathologic disease, or
a degenerative process. Traumatic spondylolisthesis may result from an acute fracture
or a stress fracture. A stress fracture typically occurs in young athletes and is distinct
from isthmic dysplastic spondylolisthesis.
The aforementioned classification systems are of little help in determining surgical
management. In 2011, the Spinal Deformity Study Group developed a classification
system that incorporated sagittal spinopelvic balance and recognized six types of
spondylolisthesis22 (Figure 6). This classification system is based on the following four
important characteristics that can be assessed on weight-bearing sagittal radiographs of
the spine and pelvis: low- or high-grade slip; low, normal, or high pelvic incidence;
balanced or unbalanced spinopelvic balance; and low or high lumbosacral kyphosis. To
classify spondylolisthesis, the slip grade is measured on a lateral standing radiograph to
determine if it is low grade (Meyerding grades 0, 1, or 2 or slip <50%) or high grade
(grades 3, 4, or spondyloptosis or slip ?50%). Sagittal balance is then measured by
determining the sacropelvic and spinopelvic alignment, using pelvic incidence, sacral
slope, pelvic tilt, and the C7 plumb line. Three types of low-grade spondylolisthesis exist.
Type 1, the nutcracker type, has a low pelvic incidence (<45°) and a low sacral slope. Type
2 has a normal pelvic incidence (between 45° and 60°). Type 3, the shear type, has a high
pelvic incidence (>60°) and a high sacral slope (Figure 4).

Figure 6 Algorithm shows the Spinal Deformity Study Group classification of
spondylolisthesis. Types 1 through 3 are low-grade spondylolisthesis, and types 4
through 6 are high-grade spondylolisthesis. Four important characteristics can be
measured on sagittal radiographs: slip, pelvic incidence (PI), spinopelvic balance, and
lumbosacral kyphosis (LSK). (Reproduced from Parent S, Labelle H, Thiong-Mac JM:
Spondylolisthesis in children and young adults, in Truumees E, Prather H, eds:
Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 371-380.)
Three types of high-grade spondylolisthesis exist. First, each patient is classified as
having a balanced or an unbalanced sacropelvic relationship using pelvic tilt and sacral
slope values or using a nomogram from a 2007 study that found that pelvic tilt and
sacral slope values were similar in control subjects, but that patients with an unbalanced
pelvis had sagittal spine alignment that differed from that of the group with a balanced
pelvis.23 If the sacral slope is greater than the pelvic tilt or if the pelvis remains within
normal values for asymptomatic patients, the pelvis is classified as balanced. If the sacral
slope is less than the pelvic tilt or when the sacral slope and pelvic tilt are below normal
values for asymptomatic patients, the pelvis is classified as unbalanced (Figure 7).

Figure 7 Lateral weight-bearing radiographs demonstrate high-grade spondylolisthesis
with a balanced (A) and unbalanced (B) pelvis. (Reproduced from Parent S, Labelle H,
Thiong-Mac JM: Spondylolisthesis in children and young adults, in Truumees E, Prather H,
eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 371-380.)
Spinopelvic balance is then determined using the C7 plumb line. If this line falls over or
behind the femoral heads, the spine is balanced, whereas if the line lies in front of the
femoral heads, the spine is unbalanced. The spine typically is balanced in patients with
low-grade spondylolisthesis and in those with high-grade spondylolisthesis with
sacropelvic balance. The three types of high-grade spondylolisthesis are as follows: type
4, balanced pelvis; type 5, unbalanced pelvis with a balanced spine; and type 6,
unbalanced pelvis with an unbalanced spine. In addition, type 5 spondylolisthesis can be
subdivided into type 5A, which is associated with normal or low lumbosacral kyphosis (as
measured by Dubousset lumbosacral angle ≥80°) and type 5B, which is associated with
high lumbosacral kyphosis (as measured by Dubousset lumbosacral angle <80°). Spinal

15/28

balance should be measured principally in patients with high-grade deformities and an
unbalanced pelvis (type 5 and type 6).
Patients with L5-S1 spondylolisthesis are a heterogeneous group with various postural
adaptations that require consideration during assessment and treatment. Abnormal
spinopelvic balance changes the biomechanical stresses at the lumbosacral junction and
affects the compensation mechanisms used to maintain adequate posture.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Mechanical low back pain
Possible radiculopathy
Physical Examination
Altered gait (pelvic waddle/Phalen-Dickson sign) and hamstring contracture
Palpable step-off
High-grade steps may present with L5 radiculopathy resulting from foraminal stenosis

Physical Examination
A careful patient history and physical examination are important for determining the
clinical extent of a deformity. Even in the presence of high-grade spondylolisthesis,
patients who do not exhibit substantial symptoms can be treated nonsurgically.
Patients with low-grade spondylolisthesis usually have a normal gait and posture. As the
slip progresses, increased lumbar lordosis with a prominent abdomen, heart-shaped
buttocks, shortened-appearing trunk, and a rib cage approaching the iliac crests may be
observed. The classic Phalen-Dickson sign occurs if the hips and knees flex to
compensate for the forward position of the trunk caused by anterior displacement of the
body’s center of gravity.24 A palpable step-off may exist at the lumbosacral junction. A
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:11 AM
AAOS | Adult Isthmic Spondylolisthesis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003014
16/28

scoliotic deformity may be observed and may be secondary to nerve root tension or
compression, muscle spasm (antalgic scoliosis), asymmetric slippage in the frontal plane
(olisthetic scoliosis), or concomitant idiopathic scoliosis. Lumbar extension often is
painful and stiff in patients with symptomatic spondylolisthesis. In some patients, tight
hamstrings may be caused by knee flexion or nerve root tension/compression,
particularly at L5. The straight leg raise test and/or the Lasègue sign usually are positive
in patients with L5 or S1 nerve root tension. Surgeons must perform a careful neurologic
examination to evaluate for signs of nerve root compression or cauda equina syndrome.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Weight-bearing radiographs may reveal a pars defect or slip.

Radiography
The clinician should obtain lateral and PA standing plain radiographs of the lumbosacral
spine in evaluating a patient for spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis. Dysplastic posterior
elements and associated scoliosis are best observed on PA radiographs. Preoperatively,
a Ferguson AP radiograph obtained parallel to the L5-S1 disk can improve visualization of
the L5 pedicles, transverse processes, and sacrum to evaluate for dysplastic features.
Postoperatively, this view may aid in evaluation of a fusion mass. A lateral radiograph
demonstrates the spondylolisthesis and allows for identification of the pars defect and
wedging of the L5 vertebral body and sacral dysplasia (Figure 1).
Plain radiographs may demonstrate a defect in as many as 75% of patients, particularly
in those with bilateral involvement. Oblique views often allow for better detection of
unilateral lesions in patients with spondylolysis. Oblique views are ordered if suspicion of
lysis cannot be excluded based on lateral radiographs; however, these views do not add
sensitivity or specificity in the detection of spondylolysis and substantially increase
radiation exposure (Resource 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:11 AM
AAOS | Adult Isthmic Spondylolisthesis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003014
17/28

In patients with spondylolisthesis, long-cassette standing PA and lateral radiographs of
the spine and pelvis, including the femoral heads, are recommended to evaluate coronal
and sagittal trunk balance. Long-cassette PA views are used to detect associated
scoliosis. Coronal balance is measured via the C7 plumb line with respect to the center of
the upper end plate of S1. Sacropelvic morphology and orientation and lumbar lordosis
and thoracic kyphosis are assessed on a long-cassette lateral radiograph. Overall sagittal
balance is assessed using the C7 plumb line with respect to the sacrum or to the hip axis.
Computed Tomography
CT can be used to help define bony morphology.

Computed Tomography
Because limited CT through the defect is associated with a radiation dose similar to that
of oblique radiography but with improved reliability, oblique radiographs should be
avoided in the pediatric population. Standard CT also is an effective imaging modality
and is associated with a lower radiation dose than bone scintigraphy. Preoperatively, CT
can be used to evaluate the bony architecture of the lumbosacral junction, with
particular attention paid to the size of the transverse processes at L4 and L5 if posterior-
only fusion is being considered (Figure 1).
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is indicated in patients who have persistent back pain with or without a neurologic
component.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is advantageous because the spine can be imaged in any plane without exposure to
radiation, and the cauda equina and nerve roots can be assessed in patients with
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:11 AM
AAOS | Adult Isthmic Spondylolisthesis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003014
18/28

neurologic compromise. MRI also can be used to evaluate T2-weighted signal change
over the pars or visualize a fracture, and MRI is more sensitive than plain radiography. In
general, MRIs must be obtained with thin section images, with T1-weighted and T2-
weighted fat-suppression MRIs obtained in axial and sagittal planes at high resolution.
T2-weghted edema in the pars corresponds with a subacute process. Particular attention
is given to evaluation of the L5 nerve roots in the L5-S1 foramen and cauda equina,
especially in patients with an elongated healed pars interarticularis. In patients with
high-grade spondylolisthesis, preoperative MRI is recommended to assess
neuroanatomic relationships and adjacent disks.
Bone Scintigraphy
Single-photon emission CT bone scintigraphy is the best imaging modality to detect
spondylolysis in patients with normal radiographs.

Bone Scintigraphy
To distinguish an acute fracture of the pars interarticularis from a long-standing defect,
bone scintigraphy may be helpful. Bone scintigraphy can help distinguish patients with
an established defect nonunion from those in whom healing is still progressing and who
may benefit from immobilization.25 Single-photon emission CT may be more accurate
and sensitive than planar bone scintigraphy because it provides more contrast and
sensitivity and improves anatomic localization of skeletal lesions;26 however, this
imaging modality results in substantial radiation exposure, with organ radiation doses
that are five times higher than those with focal CT. Because first-line management for
most spondylolysis is nonsurgical, the benefits of this type of imaging should be carefully
weighed.
Management
Nonsurgical Management

Most patients improve with activity modifications and physical therapy, including hamstring
stretching, lumbar flexibility, and core strengthening.
Brace management (antilordosis) can be used in children and adolescents.
Most pars defects persist radiographically despite the resolution of symptoms.

Nonsurgical Management
Asymptomatic individuals with an incidental finding of spondylolysis or low-grade low-
dysplastic developmental spondylolisthesis require no treatment or activity restrictions;
however, these patients are at greater risk for progression and should be seen at regular
intervals (6 months) for radiographic surveillance until skeletal maturity. In skeletally
immature patient with a slip of less than 50%, nonsurgical treatment is recommended.
Usually, a good or excellent outcome is achieved, and the patient can return to sports
activity. Nonsurgical management of acute symptoms includes primarily rest, physical
therapy (lumbar and abdominal muscle training), hamstring stretching, mild analgesic
agents, and NSAIDs. Symptomatic patients with focal increased uptake observed on a
bone scan, single-photon emission CT, or MRI and, more specifically, patients with an
acquired stress fracture, may respond to a trial of bracing and rest to unite the pars
defect. Healing infrequently occurs but is more likely to occur in patients with acute or
unilateral defects. Cessation of sporting activities is more closely associated with a
positive outcome than achieving bony union. Defects associated with chronic-appearing
unilateral lesions, bilateral disease, and spondylolisthesis are less likely to heal. Bracing
in neutral lordosis with the use of a thoracolumbosacral orthosis worn full-time for 2 to 3
months is recommended and can be attempted for pain alleviation in some
symptomatic patients with chronic spondylolysis. Unfortunately, no high-level evidence
exists on specific recommendations or protocols for nonsurgical management.
Surgical Management
In situ posterolateral L5-S1 fusion is indicated in children and adolescents with low-grade (less
than 50% slip) spondylolisthesis.
Pars repair is indicated in persistently symptomatic patients with spondylosis with minimal
degenerative disk disease, no slippage, and no discogenic component to their pain.

Fusion is indicated for high-grade slips in most children and adolescents irrespective of
symptoms.
In adults with persistent symptoms, surgical treatment is superior to nonsurgical treatment.
For adult grade 1 and 2 slips, the role of anterior column support has not been well defined.
Similarly, controversy exists with regard to the benefits of circumferential versus
posterolateral fusion alone. For adult grade 3 and 4 slips, evidence supports higher fusion
rates with anterior column support.
Partial reduction and transosseous fusions for high-grade spondylolisthesis result in
predictably good outcomes.
The role of complete reduction has not yet been established.
The last 50% of reduction is associated with the greatest neurologic risk.

Surgical Management
Surgical treatment is indicated for slips greater than 50% in growing children and slips
greater than 75% in mature adolescents, in patients with documented slip progression
of more than 30%, patients with persistent functional impairment, patients with pain or
neurologic symptoms despite appropriate nonsurgical treatment, and patients with
progressive postural deformity or gait abnormality. Patients with slip grades of 3 or
higher usually are candidates for surgical treatment.
Patients with low-grade spondylolisthesis usually can be treated via postural reduction
and in situ fusion. The need for decompression can be determined based on the
patient’s symptoms and physical examination findings, with additional information
obtained from advanced imaging studies (CT and/or MRI). Central canal stenosis and/or
foraminal stenosis should be ruled out and, if present, formal or indirect decompression
should be performed. In situ fusion can be achieved via a Wiltse approach (if no formal
central decompression is required) or via a central midline approach. Posterolateral
fusion with autologous iliac crest bone graft remains the preferred procedure for in situ
fusion. If feasible, spinal instrumentation reduces the need for prolonged
immobilization; however, the space available for bone grafting is reduced (Figure 8;
Video 3).

The treatment of patients with high-grade spondylolisthesis remains somewhat
controversial. Some historical cohort studies have reported high complication rates with
attempted reduction.27,28 In addition, excellent clinical outcomes at long-term follow-up
of in situ fusion recently have been reported.29 With advancements in neuromonitoring,
surgical instrumentation, and understanding of normal and pathologic sagittal balance, a
subset of patients with high-grade spondylolisthesis are increasingly likely to benefit
from reduction procedures. A clear distinction must be made between a well-balanced,
high-grade spondylolisthesis (type 4) and an unbalanced, high-grade spondylolisthesis
(types 5 or 6). The balanced type 4 spondylolisthesis may be fused in situ after postural
reduction on the operating table with the addition of pedicle and iliac screws. The fusion
can be strengthened by a fibular strut graft and/or by intervertebral screws spanning the
L5-S1 space from an S1 posteriorly based starting point.
In patients with a high-grade spondylolisthesis with pelvic retroversion with or without
sagittal spinal imbalance (types 5 or 6), normal sagittal balance cannot be restored
without correcting the lumbosacral kyphosis and decreasing the pelvic tilt or
retroversion. The most important technical aspects are that the L5 nerve root should be
widely decompressed and well visualized before any attempted reduction, and every
effort should be made to correct lumbosacral kyphosis to decrease tension on the
nerves and facilitate reduction. A sacral dome osteotomy may be required to aid in
lumbosacral kyphosis reduction. Complete reduction of the slip is not mandatory. To
help reduce the risk of pseudarthrosis, anterior support in the form of an interbody cage
often is used in combination with posteriorly based pedicle screws, with or without
additional iliac fixation (Figure 9; Video 4).
Spondyloptosis (complete slippage of L5 over S1) is the most severe type of translational
spine deformity, and severe neurologic symptoms usually develop. Spondyloptosis is
one of the most challenging surgical problems. Because the slippage is complete,
surgical reduction of L5 over S1 usually is not possible. Proposed treatment options
